content:
Hold on until the last moment

"To be frank, I held on until the last moment." Ms. Yuen and her elder sister grew up in Wang Fuk Court with their parents. Their father later passed away and her sister got married, so she lived with her mother alone until the fire. Her mother died in the blaze. While returning to her flat during the recovery period, she once wore a sweater printed with the words "rebuild on the original site" to voice her demand. Yet the authorities rejected it and the owners' corporation refused to put it on the agenda, and it was only one week before the acquisition deadline of 31 August that she finally submitted a "letter of acceptance of the acquisition offer".

Ms. Yuen believes Wang Fuk Court residents have already been "crushed by a rock" — there was no way out. She said the two briefing officers she had dealt with could not answer her questions and had only one clear objective: to press residents on whether they would sell their flats.

Life after the disaster is "living as a lodger"

Since the fire, Ms. Yuen has first moved into Shan Lau in Tai Po and then into Yue Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a "temporary residence fee" every month. The original bed, dining table, TV cabinet in the unit, as well as the neighbours and security guard, all keep reminding her of who she is. She describes her life after the incident as "living as a lodger".

Reflecting on what "home" really means

Every day after work, she does not get back to this empty flat until eight or nine o'clock, and on holidays she chooses to leave and go to her sister's place. "Actually, after the incident, I have already started thinking: what does 'home' mean, what does 'a house' mean? A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when this home in Wang Fuk Court has been burned down by someone…"

"The word 'home' is quite heavy for me now"

When the reporter asked Ms. Yuen about her idea of home, she said the old phone that still held photos of Wang Fuk Court had also been lost in the fire, and all the memories exist only in her mind. She sighed deeply: "A home is not just about having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom and a full set of home appliances for me, that already counts as a so-called proper home. It makes me rethink what the elements of a proper home are, so I cannot answer this question for now, because the word 'home' is quite heavy for me now."

Dissatisfied with officials' 'declutter' remarks

Officials' responses to the Wang Fuk Court fire — for instance, Chief Secretary for Administration Deputy Cheuk Wing-hing's "declutter" remark, and Financial Secretary Deputy Wong Wai-lun's talk about market value and so on — have only deepened her helplessness and anger. "The more silent you are, the less I understand." "Actually, when they can say something so cold and thin, what on earth is their idea of the meaning of home?"

A sense of being 'sold off cheap'

Recalling the moment she signed the letter of acceptance, Ms. Yuen said the worst feeling in her heart was unwillingness and a sense of injustice — a feeling of being "sold off cheap" — because home is not just about monetary value, it is also a bond of emotion and memory. "The unit was something my dad and mum built up through hard work. If it really has to be taken from us at no value, compared with being 'sold off cheap' now, I am even more unwilling to accept it."

After signing the letter, Ms. Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee will not submit its report until October. Ms. Yuen says pursuing accountability is one part of it, "but how a person can find closure, I cannot answer. Because from the incident until now, life feels like a total loss. First, the home was burned down, and the meaning of it being burned is like wiping away the entire history of my growing up; a family member also died in the fire, and it was a sudden death… there is a huge hole in my heart. Can anything really fill this hole? Or will there be a day when it can heal? I don't know how to answer."
